title: A South African Language Teacher Educator's Reflective Journey Through Sociocultural Theory and Asset‐Based Mediation
text_snippet: A South African Language Teacher Educator's Reflective Journey Through Sociocultural Theory and Asset‐Based Mediation Abstract This reflective article chronicles a South African English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI) university teacher educator's journey from professional disillusionment toward a more intentional, transformative praxis. The catalyst for this journey was the recurring observation of novice teachers abandoning dialogic, asset‐based pedagogies learned in pre‐service preparation and reverting to authoritarian, monolingual transmission under systemic classroom pressures. This “disappearing practice” highlighted the limitations of a transactional teacher education model that transmitted “best practices” without fundamentally reorganizing teachers' internalized reasoning and stance. In response, I engage in a theoretical reorientation, drawing deeply on Vygotskian Sociocultural Theory (VSCT) as applied to second language teacher education, particularly Johnson, Verity, & Childs (2025) tripartite framework of innovation, intentionality, and intervention . This lens reframes teacher resistance and cognitive‐emotional dissonance not as problems, but as vital “drama” and engines of development. title: Exploring Teacher Idealism: The Concentric Model, Narrative Identity, and Agency in English Language Teaching in Türkiye
text_snippet: Exploring Teacher Idealism: The Concentric Model, Narrative Identity, and Agency in English Language Teaching in Türkiye Abstract Teacher idealism, the ethical, aspirational, and future‐oriented dimension of professional identity, remains under‐theorized in second language teacher education (SLTE) despite its central role in sustaining pedagogical agency and professional resilience. Drawing on the Concentric Model of Teacher Idealism (Özmen & Harmandaoğlu Baz, 2026), this narrative inquiry examines how three in‐service English language teachers in Türkiye narrate, sustain, and enact teacher idealism amid intensifying systemic demands. text_snippet: Understanding STEM Coursetaking Among English Learner Subgroups: Longitudinal Evidence From Four State Policy Contexts Abstract Although a substantial body of research documents the problem of course tracking for students classified as English learners (ELs), very little work has addressed the notably different challenges that subgroups of ELs face across different state policy contexts. This descriptive study uses a cross‐state, comparative framework to explore how graduation and reclassification policies in New York City, Oregon, Texas, and Michigan relate to ELs' access to college‐preparatory math and science coursework. title: Neoliberalism, Standard Language Ideology, and Native‐Speakerism in South Korean K‐12 English Education Policy: Evidence from Government Documents and an Elementary Textbook
text_snippet: Neoliberalism, Standard Language Ideology, and Native‐Speakerism in South Korean K‐12 English Education Policy: Evidence from Government Documents and an Elementary Textbook Abstract Language ideologies shape English education policy in South Korea and influence learners' identities as language users. Prior research has primarily examined policy documents through the lens of neoliberalism, or textbooks with a focus on cultural representation, treating these as separate domains. In contrast, this study takes a multilayered perspective, tracing how neoliberalism, standard language ideology, and native‐speakerism interrelate across government policy, including national curricula and press releases from 2015 to 2023, and a 2025 third‐grade English textbook based on these policies. title: Effects of GenAI ‐Assisted Digital Multimodal Composing on Students' Second Language Writing Performance: A Quasi‐Experimental Study
text_snippet: Effects of GenAI ‐Assisted Digital Multimodal Composing on Students' Second Language Writing Performance: A Quasi‐Experimental Study Abstract There have been mixed perceptions about the effect of digital multimodal composing (DMC) on learners' second language (L2) writing performance. This debate is reshaped as generative AI (GenAI) transforms both text‐based writing and DMC processes, which may affect their impacts on L2 writing performance. This 14‐week quasi‐experimental study compares students' L2 writing performance development in GenAI‐assisted DMC, GenAI‐assisted text‐based writing, and text‐based writing conditions. A total of 161 Chinese university students from three intact classes were randomly assigned to three instructional groups: GenAI‐assisted DMC (54 students), GenAI‐assisted text‐based writing (57 students), and a text‐based writing group (50 students). The DMC group received instruction in creating two digital posters, whereas the other two groups were guided to write two 150‐word essays. title: Alignment and Creative Extension in EFL Learners' Multimodal Composing: A Case Analysis of Audiovisual Continuation Tasks
text_snippet: Alignment and Creative Extension in EFL Learners' Multimodal Composing: A Case Analysis of Audiovisual Continuation Tasks Abstract Multimodal literacy has become essential for professional communication; however, EFL pedagogies of digital multimodal composing (DMC) have primarily emphasized independent production, paying less attention to how learners compose in response to authentic multimodal input. Conceptualized as a type of DMC and grounded in the xu ‐argument, audiovisual continuation tasks integrate multimodal comprehension with production by inviting learners to interpret authentic source input and align with and creatively extend it through continued meaning‐making. Drawing on this framing, this study examines how EFL learners align with and creatively extend source input across semiotic and content dimensions in audiovisual continuation tasks. Twenty‐six first‐year Business English majors created continuation videos based on an original video titled “What is a Brand,” following a TBLT framework that combined comprehension, scripting, and video production with peer and teacher feedback. title: Multiliteracies in Action: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Develop Digital Multimodal Composing Tasks for Multilingual Learners of English Through Technology‐Mediated Task‐Based Language Teaching
text_snippet: Multiliteracies in Action: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Develop Digital Multimodal Composing Tasks for Multilingual Learners of English Through Technology‐Mediated Task‐Based Language Teaching Abstract Digital multimodal composing (DMC), which includes digital storytelling and writing, has grown markedly with the increasing use of technology in the second language (L2) classroom. Although much of this research is grounded in sociocultural approaches, recent studies have taken a cognitive interactionist approach to explore how DMC can promote noticing and peer interaction. However, few studies exploring DMC have utilized technology‐mediated task‐based language teaching (TMTBLT) as a methodological and pedagogical framework. Addressing calls by previous scholars to explore multiliteracies with DMC task design, this study qualitatively explores how multimodal generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support DMC and learners' task engagement. Drawing from a multiliteracies framework, this study examines how 10 upper‐beginning ESL learners used GenAI to generate visuals for meaningful, authentic DMC tasks in which they collaboratively designed artifacts for future students navigating life in Hawaiʻi. title: Tracing Longitudinal Changes in Learners' Experience and Performance During Microsoft Copilot Voice‐Supported English Speaking Practice
text_snippet: Tracing Longitudinal Changes in Learners' Experience and Performance During Microsoft Copilot Voice‐Supported English Speaking Practice Abstract This article reports a one‐group time‐series study of Microsoft Copilot Voice (MCV) as a structural scaffold in a mandatory university English course in China. Sixty‐eight environmental engineering undergraduates participated in an MCV‐supported speaking sequence embedded in regular instruction. Oral performance and six dimensions of second language learning experience (L2LE)—positive emotions, negative emotions, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment—were measured at three time points: pre‐task, main task, and post‐task. Results from latent growth curve modeling showed significant positive slopes for oral performance and the positive L2LE dimensions, together with a significant negative slope for negative emotions. title: Supporting Young Foreign Language Learners With Image Generative AI in Digital Multimodal Composing: Benefits and Challenges
text_snippet: Supporting Young Foreign Language Learners With Image Generative AI in Digital Multimodal Composing: Benefits and Challenges Abstract Integrating generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into digital multimodal composing (DMC) offers promising avenues for young Foreign Language (FL) learners' learning experiences. Image‐based GenAI tools enable students to generate personalized images from written prompts to help convey meanings, and DMC combines text, images, and sound to create meaning. However, most existing research on GenAI and DMC focuses on text‐based GenAI use and older learners, leaving image GenAI usage and younger primary school students underexplored. This action research addressed this gap by designing a DMC task for primary school FL students ( N = 33, aged 8–9) using image‐based GenAI. Students engaged in structured pre‐writing tasks applied prompt‐engineering strategies targeting key language features and AI‐generated images to support idea visualization and creative expression. Peer evaluation further fostered collaborative feedback. Classroom video recordings, group interviews, and AI‐generated images revealed positive reactions, including sustained engagement, enhanced agency, and spontaneous collaboration, even though challenges with prompting GenAI for specific outputs were noted.

title: Curbing Boredom in University EFL Classrooms: Findings From a Multimethod Intervention
text_snippet: Curbing Boredom in University EFL Classrooms: Findings From a Multimethod Intervention Abstract Boredom has emerged as a salient classroom emotion in L2 learning, yet intervention studies testing whether it can be reduced remain scarce. This quasi‐experimental study investigated a 12‐week boredom‐regulation intervention in university EFL classes in Saudi Arabia. Four teachers and 106 male students participated, with classes assigned to experimental or control conditions. Repeated‐measure analyses and ANCOVAs showed significant declines in self‐reported boredom in the experimental group and increases in the control group. title: Tracing Adaptive Transfer Across Genres and Media: GenAI ‐Supported ESL Learners' Digital Multimodal Composing and Traditional Writing Practices
text_snippet: Tracing Adaptive Transfer Across Genres and Media: GenAI ‐Supported ESL Learners' Digital Multimodal Composing and Traditional Writing Practices Abstract Drawing on the adaptive transfer and the genre knowledge model as a conceptual framework, this research explores how English as a second language (ESL) learners transferred knowledge across genres (narration and argumentation) and media (print‐based writing and video) with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) platforms in the new era of multimodal unified comprehension and generation. The GenAI platforms included text‐to‐text, text‐to‐image, text‐to‐music, text‐to‐video, and text‐conditioned relighting GenAI models, ranging from Microsoft Copilot, Pika, MusicFX, to IC Light. Data were collected from three PhD students' text‐based products, digital multimodal composing (DMC) texts, post‐task interviews, and the first author's observations in a 15‐week extracurricular digital writing program at a public university in Auckland. title: Well‐Being Trajectories of Pre‐Service Language Teachers During the Practicum: An Ecological Analysis
text_snippet: Well‐Being Trajectories of Pre‐Service Language Teachers During the Practicum: An Ecological Analysis Abstract Learning to teach is an emotionally challenging endeavor. Yet, despite increasing interest in teachers' well‐being more broadly, relatively little is known about how it unfolds over time within identity‐forming contexts such as the practicum, particularly in the case of pre‐service language teachers (PSLTs). Addressing this gap, the present practicum‐based study adopted an ecological approach to examine the well‐being trajectories of three Polish PSLTs during their mandatory school placement. Participants' well‐being during early teaching episodes was tracked over 2 weeks using same‐day video‐assisted retrospective ratings at five‐minute intervals. These ratings were complemented by in‐depth interviews conducted twice per week and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. The findings suggest that PSLTs' well‐being exhibited considerable variability both within lessons and across teaching sessions. title: Teacher Perceptions of GenAI ‐Integrated Digital Storytelling for Refugee‐Background Youth
text_snippet: Teacher Perceptions of GenAI ‐Integrated Digital Storytelling for Refugee‐Background Youth Abstract Digital storytelling (DST), the composing of 2–3 minute first‐person digital multimodal narratives, integrating photographs, video clips, voice‐over, text, and music related to personal experiences, is arguably one of the most powerful forms of digital multimodal composing (DMC). Expanding the range of modes (e.g., images, sounds, multiple languages) through which they can share their personal experiences, DST can be particularly transformative for refugee‐background youth. As GenAI is increasingly integrated into DMC practices, its potential impact on DST, particularly for refugee‐background youth, needs to be examined. Guided by sociomaterial and multimodal approaches to literacies, this empirical, qualitative case study examines the perceptions of seven Canadian English as an Additional Language teachers regarding GenAI‐integrated DST for the education of refugee‐background youth, through engaging the teachers in their own GenAI‐integrated DST. text_snippet: Affective Repertoires and Motivation in L2 and L3 Learning: An AI ‐Augmented Mixed Methods Study Abstract This study investigates the enjoyment, anxiety, and motivation of Turkish high school learners in L2 English and L3 Spanish foreign language classes using an explanatory sequential mixed methods design. Quantitative data were collected from 115 students using the Foreign Language Enjoyment (FLE), Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety (FLCA), and Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB) scales. Findings showed significantly higher enjoyment and anxiety in Spanish, while English elicited greater motivation. To explore the deeper underlying causes, focus group interviews were analyzed through AI‐assisted Sentiment Analysis (SA), followed by thematic analysis. SA enabled efficient pre‐clustering of learner statements by emotional polarity and supported integration through merging. Qualitative findings revealed an affect‐motivation mismatch: Spanish was more enjoyable due to creative pedagogy but triggered anxiety linked to low proficiency; English was less engaging but perceived as essential for future goals. title: Late‐Arriving Multilingual Learners' Transition from K–16 Education to the Workforce: Cultural Capital and Habitus Adaptation across Fields
text_snippet: Late‐Arriving Multilingual Learners' Transition from K–16 Education to the Workforce: Cultural Capital and Habitus Adaptation across Fields Abstract English learners (ELs) in US K–12 schools face systemic barriers that constrain their college and career readiness. Although research has richly documented ELs' limited opportunities to learn in high school and barriers to postsecondary education, much less is known about how late‐arriving ELs move from high school to community college (CC) and then into the workforce. This longitudinal qualitative multiple‐case study follows four late‐arriving multilingual learners (MLs), all of whom were classified as ELs in high school, over 6 years, as they moved from high school through CC and into the workforce. title: Navigating Between the Scylla and Charybdis of Hype and Fear: Decolonizing ELT Materials Through Generative Artificial Intelligence
text_snippet: Navigating Between the Scylla and Charybdis of Hype and Fear: Decolonizing ELT Materials Through Generative Artificial Intelligence Abstract Despite calls from critical applied linguists to decolonize ELT materials that reproduce colonial ideologies, teachers working under neoliberal constraints and attendant time pressures often have to deliver textbook content as is rather than revising it. This study explores to what extent a state‐of‐the‐art large language model (LLM) can work as a practical tool for decolonizing materials. We focus on a textbook unit widely used in Hong Kong that reproduces a white savior narrative and stereotypical representation of Africa and Africans as a telling case of coloniality. The unit was processed through an LLM with a decolonizing prompt, and both the original and AI‐revised versions were subjected to critical discourse analysis to understand how social actors and actions are represented and constructed at the macro and micro levels. title: Centering Structural and Systemic Barriers in Rethinking College and Career Readiness for Students Classified as English Learners
text_snippet: Centering Structural and Systemic Barriers in Rethinking College and Career Readiness for Students Classified as English Learners Abstract College and career readiness has been prominent in educational policy discourses in the United States for the past few decades. However, students classified as English learners (ELs) have rarely factored into these policy considerations and have faced considerable structural and systemic barriers that have limited their educational opportunities. This special issue brings together empirical work that centers ELs in college and career readiness. Importantly, these papers highlight barriers to ELs' college and career readiness and present potential directions for redressing these structural and systemic inequities.

title: Ethical Concerns in GenAI ‐Assisted Collaborative Digital Multimodal Composing: A Case Study of Blended Learning
text_snippet: Ethical Concerns in GenAI ‐Assisted Collaborative Digital Multimodal Composing: A Case Study of Blended Learning Abstract While providing affordances for digital multimodal composing (DMC), GenAI brings along various ethical concerns. Prior research has discussed algorithmic risks and technology‐related design issues, yet little attention has been paid to how learners collectively perceive and respond to ethical issues. This qualitative case study explored how eight English learners perceived and responded to ethical concerns over a semester of GenAI‐assisted academic poster‐making in a blended learning context. Data from classroom discussions, GenAI logs, and interviews revealed three key dimensions of ethical concerns: legal, social, and pedagogical. Students' ethical concerns progressed from abstract and superficial awareness to contextualized and task‐specific understandings. Their responses to ethical concerns evolved from reactive, individual, vague responses to proactive, collaborative negotiations, and shared responsibility. Cognitive, experiential, and social factors, including metacognitive awareness, practical engagement, and peer collaboration, contributed to the progression. title: Linguistically Responsive Instruction in a PhD ‐Level EMI Course: A Qualitative Case Study from Thailand
text_snippet: Linguistically Responsive Instruction in a PhD ‐Level EMI Course: A Qualitative Case Study from Thailand Abstract This study examined how an experienced Thai instructor in a PhD‐level EMI course implemented linguistically responsive instruction (LRI) to support student learning, the rationales behind his practices, and students' perceptions of them. Data from classroom observations and instructor and student interviews were analyzed and interpreted through an LRI lens. The findings suggested that the instructor employed a range of LRI practices to help students meet the epistemic demands of PhD education and develop as competent members of their academic community. Participating students valued these practices and did not perceive them as English language support. Compared to prior LRI‐informed research, which primarily focused on undergraduate settings, the study suggests that LRI at the PhD level may have a broader scope and operate at the course level rather than solely at the lesson level. title: From Relevant to Publishable in TESOL Research: Contribution, Access, and Accountability
text_snippet: From Relevant to Publishable in TESOL Research: Contribution, Access, and Accountability Abstract Many manuscripts sent to TQ are recognizably TESOL, carefully written, and ethically serious. The harder editorial question is what moves a manuscript from relevant to publishable. In this editorial, we argue that publishability rests on three connected expectations. The article needs to make a contribution that changes how TESOL researchers, teachers, teacher educators, or policymakers understand a problem. It needs to make knowledge accessible beyond a narrow group of specialists, including through clearer writing and the continued use of OASIS summaries for accepted articles. It also needs to make its claims accountable, through responsible data practices, transparent methods, careful use of AI, and authorial ownership of the argument. These expectations have consequences for authors deciding where to send their work, for reviewers deciding what deserves space in the journal, and for us as editors of a journal that helps shape what the field recognizes as valuable TESOL research.

title: Navigating Barriers, Leveraging Capital: English Learners' Experiences in College
text_snippet: Navigating Barriers, Leveraging Capital: English Learners' Experiences in College Abstract English learners (ELs) have high aspirations for postsecondary education, yet many do not complete a college degree, suggesting that they often encounter obstacles to fulfilling their goals in college. To better understand the factors that create barriers to postsecondary success among ELs, this paper draws on data gathered during an 18‐month critical ethnography of 16 ELs and 4 staff members at a community college in upstate New York. Through Bourdieu's framework of cultural capital, findings detail how participants often felt underprepared for both the academic and institutional challenges they encountered at college. Many students also experienced obstacles as they attempted to balance their education with a daunting work schedule. Despite these difficulties, participants leveraged varied forms of nondominant capital as they sought to overcome the obstacles they encountered. This paper calls attention to the resources and assets ELs possess while providing useful insights into institutional arrangements and policies which are needed to ensure that ELs are ready not only for college coursework but are also prepared to navigate the college process.

title: Beyond Static Measures: The Impact of Lexical Stress Error Categories on IELTS Spoken Proficiency
text_snippet: Beyond Static Measures: The Impact of Lexical Stress Error Categories on IELTS Spoken Proficiency Abstract Although current pedagogical practices and research recognize that lexical stress errors can affect proficiency scores, they have thus far treated such errors as a single category. This paper explored the impact of various categories of stress errors, as proposed in the English Word Stress Error Gravity Hierarchy (Ghosh & Levis, 2021), on IELTS spoken proficiency. title: The Hare and the Tortoise in Ecological L2 Learning: Distributed Practice Effects in Vocabulary and Grammar
text_snippet: The Hare and the Tortoise in Ecological L2 Learning: Distributed Practice Effects in Vocabulary and Grammar Abstract Research on the distributed practice effect, that is the impact of different intervals between learning sessions, has investigated both intentional and incidental learning of second language vocabulary and grammar targets. This research is complex and has produced conflicting findings: whereas robust effects have been shown for intentional vocabulary learning, evidence for incidental and grammar learning are less clear. The present experiment combines intentional vocabulary and incidental grammar targets in L2 English, and compares participants working at 2‐ and 7‐day intervals on an online platform designed to provide contextualized and pedagogically sound learning activities. Results of vocabulary knowledge ( N = 72) and acceptability judgment ( N = 70) tests showed significant vocabulary learning under intentional conditions, but no significant incidental grammar learning. Experimental design and pedagogical implications are discussed.

Eight participants from a senior high school completed the task and participated in think‐aloud protocols as well as semi‐structured interviews. The data were analyzed using a causal network framework. title: “Just My Presence, Just Using These Words Is Not Enough”: Shifting from Identity‐Based Inclusion to Structural Transformation in Language Education
text_snippet: “Just My Presence, Just Using These Words Is Not Enough”: Shifting from Identity‐Based Inclusion to Structural Transformation in Language Education Abstract This study focuses on 17 in‐service language teachers who graduated from a social justice‐oriented MA program in Teaching Languages to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) and Teaching Foreign Languages (TFL) at a US higher education institution. Drawing on multiple data sources that connect participants' pre‐service and in‐service experiences, the study provides a longitudinal perspective on how they enacted social justice language education (SJLE) at least 1 year after completing their program. Findings show that participants' understandings of social justice were largely grounded in identity politics, and their social justice pedagogies primarily focused on diversity and inclusion. Their inclusive practices involved recognizing and affirming learners' identities, promoting awareness of cultural and identity‐based differences, and modeling inclusive language use. title: Exploring Distribution‐of‐Practice Effects on L2 Grammar Learning Among Older Adults
text_snippet: Exploring Distribution‐of‐Practice Effects on L2 Grammar Learning Among Older Adults Abstract This paper examines the effects of practice distribution among older adult learners of L2 English, an understudied population in both second language acquisition and distributed practice research. Additionally, it considers the effects of proficiency and age. Healthy older adults ( N = 53) aged between 56 and 78 years learned the simple past and present perfect in L2 English over three classroom‐based lessons with either a 3.5‐day or 7‐day intersession interval (ISI). Their knowledge of the target forms was tested through a grammaticality judgment test at two retention intervals (RIs) of 7 and 21 days. Results showed no main effect of ISI and no interaction between ISI and RI, in contrast to prior research with college‐aged participants using similar tasks. Similarly, proficiency did not interact with ISI. However, a significant main effect of age was found with younger participants outperforming older participants. text_snippet: Harnessing GenAI for EFL Oral Presentations: Releasing Cognitive Resources to Foster Critical Thinking, Enjoyment, and Motivation Abstract While generative artificial intelligence tools have been increasingly integrated into language education to optimize learners' learning outcomes, the effects of ChatGPT on EFL learners' oral presentation performance, critical thinking, enjoyment, and motivation have not been fully explored. Although traditional AI chatbots have shown potential in language learning support, their reliance on fixed interaction paths and limited capacity for human‐like dialogue have constrained their effectiveness in cognitively demanding tasks such as oral presentation preparation. To address this gap, this study drew on Activity Theory (AT) as a theoretical lens to examine how generative AI (GenAI) mediates EFL oral presentation preparation in flipped classrooms. A quasi‐experiment was conducted to evaluate the effects of GenAI intervention. Two intact classes with 99 EFL students (without GenAI experiences) were randomly assigned to either an experimental ( n = 49) or control ( n = 50) group. The experimental group (EG) used both search engines and ChatGPT, while the control group (CG) only used search engines. title: “It's Not Equality, …It's Not Humanizing:” Content‐Area Teachers' Tensions Between CCR Curriculum and Linguistically Responsive Professional Development
text_snippet: “It's Not Equality, …It's Not Humanizing:” Content‐Area Teachers' Tensions Between CCR Curriculum and Linguistically Responsive Professional Development Abstract This qualitative study explores how secondary content‐area teachers of emergent bilingual (EB) students navigate tensions between linguistically responsive professional development (PD) and the implementation of state‐mandated College and Career Readiness (CCR) curricula in south Texas. It draws on data from coaching sessions and individual interviews with three educators who participated in Project SELFIES, a PD initiative intended to promote critically informed and linguistically responsive pedagogies among secondary educators serving EB students. Focusing on middle school context, which is under‐researched in CCR literature, the study examines how teachers experience and respond to CCR‐aligned curricular mandates such as Energize and Ascend Learning. Based on the thematic data analysis, the findings demonstrate how the three content‐area teachers experienced and responded to conflicting expectations, systemic constraints, and their own evolving identities as critical educators. title: The Longitudinal Relationship Between Language Learning Enjoyment and Out‐of‐Class Exposure: A Random‐Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Analysis of Junior Secondary School English Learners
text_snippet: The Longitudinal Relationship Between Language Learning Enjoyment and Out‐of‐Class Exposure: A Random‐Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Analysis of Junior Secondary School English Learners Abstract Foreign language (FL) enjoyment and out‐of‐class FL learning have garnered much attention from both researchers and frontline educators in recent years. The current study set out to contribute to these two burgeoning areas by examining specifically the longitudinal relationships between two types of FL enjoyment (classroom private and out‐of‐class informal learning (ILE)) and voluntary out‐of‐class FL exposure across three timepoints over 1.5 years. 366 Grade‐7 EFL learners from Hong Kong completed three questionnaires and six mini‐surveys. Extending the traditional cross‐lagged panel modeling (CLPM) approach, we adopted a more rigorous and novel method, known as Random‐Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Modeling (RI‐CLPM), which takes into account between‐person and within‐person variances when examining relationships. The findings revealed that private enjoyment and exposure time, but not ILE, demonstrated significant autoregressive relationships. More importantly, preceding within‐person ILE significantly predicted subsequent exposure time, but not the other way around. title: Contingencies of Extended Response‐Pursuit Practices in L2 Listening Classroom Interaction
text_snippet: Contingencies of Extended Response‐Pursuit Practices in L2 Listening Classroom Interaction Abstract Student participation in L2 classroom interaction is paramount in foreign language learning, yet teachers often encounter silence after posing questions. When student contributions are minimal or absent, teachers deploy response‐pursuit practices to maintain pedagogical progressivity. Although there exists a significant amount of research highlighting the importance of response‐pursuit practices, to our best knowledge, there still exists a gap in terms of how and when extended response‐pursuit practices may or may not culminate in student responses. Thus, using multimodal conversation analysis, we aim to bridge this gap by documenting how and to what extent extended response‐pursuit practices may trigger student participation in an EFL listening classroom, a context relatively underexamined from a micro‐analytic perspective. The data consist of 41 hours of video‐recorded EFL classroom interaction in higher education. This study holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of the contingencies of response‐pursuit moves in an L2 listening classroom interaction and provides implications for Classroom Interactional Competence (CIC) and L2 teacher education.

title: Situating the Story: Guiding EFL Learners to Use Orientation in Narrative Writing
text_snippet: Situating the Story: Guiding EFL Learners to Use Orientation in Narrative Writing Abstract This article presents a classroom‐based instructional cycle designed to support university‐level EFL learners in developing narrative writing through a targeted focus on orientation—the discourse component that situates a narrative in time, place, and character. Grounded in Labov's narrative framework and sociocultural theories of learning, the cycle integrates explicit instruction, peer evaluation, and guided reflection to support discourse‐level organization. Students first completed a narrative retelling task based on a short silent film; initial drafts frequently began with action, often omitting essential orientation elements. A mini‐lecture, model texts, and peer‐led discussion then guided learners in noticing and revising their use of orientation. In a subsequent task, students applied an analytic rubric to evaluate peer writing and compared their assessments with instructor ratings, promoting metacognitive engagement and deeper awareness of how orientation shapes reader interpretation. title: Avoiding De‐Skilling and Dependency: A Practical Guide to Using Generative AI in TESOL Teacher Education
text_snippet: Avoiding De‐Skilling and Dependency: A Practical Guide to Using Generative AI in TESOL Teacher Education Abstract This focused article argues that generative AI (GenAI) in TESOL teacher education (TTE) must be reconceptualized to address the risk of teacher de‐skilling and GenAI dependency. Otherwise, teachers may offload professional work onto GenAI before developing evidence‐informed pedagogies and safeguards. Drawing on the five dimensions of professional GenAI competence (P‐GenAI‐C), we outline how TTE programs can organize sustainable teacher learning for the GenAI age. We then offer practical design principles and activities for pre‐service and in‐service contexts, including low‐stakes tool engagement, scenario‐based microteaching, feedback routines, and structured reflection. Across these approaches, we emphasize teacher agency, transparency, and ethical responsibility, including attention to digital exclusion, labor conditions, and environmental impacts. We argue that effective GenAI integration is predicated on teacher competence and professional judgment.

title: Scholarship on English Learners' College and Career Readiness: How Far We Have Come and How Much More We Have to Go
text_snippet: Scholarship on English Learners' College and Career Readiness: How Far We Have Come and How Much More We Have to Go Abstract Scholarship on English learners' college and career readiness has made significant progress over the past 15 years or so, and this Special Issue is a good example of the latest research in this area. In this afterword, I first discuss four developments as evidenced in the Special Issue articles: (a) the use of richly varied theoretical frameworks, (b) progress in qualitative inquiry, (c) a broader scope of both grade spans and stakeholders, and (d) an emphasis on solutions. I then identify questions and issues that remain understudied and that we, as a group of scholars committed to ELs' equitable access to postsecondary education and career pathways, must collectively explore further, including (a) interrogating the concept of college and career readiness itself and (b) identifying and building systemic solutions.

title: Lexical Syllabus in Elementary and Secondary Education: Construction and Implementation
text_snippet: Lexical Syllabus in Elementary and Secondary Education: Construction and Implementation Abstract Nonnative language users operate with significantly limited vocabularies compared to native speakers, particularly when the language is learnt in school contexts. This paper demonstrates how empirical research on vocabulary learning combined with experience in teaching and curricula design has informed the principled construction of a lexical syllabus for Israeli elementary and secondary education (Grades 4–12, CEFR Pre‐A1–B2) in 2020, subsequently implemented in school textbooks, in 2023. Syllabus construction was guided by considerations regarding the amount of lexis necessary for performing language tasks, word frequencies, orthographic patterns, multiword units, distinction between receptive and productive knowledge, and word organization units. Implementation was informed by research on the effects of repeated exposures, spacing and recycling, and optimal types of vocabulary activities.

title: Incorporating a Global Englishes Language Teaching ( GELT ) Perspective in Taiwanese Elementary Classrooms: Teachers' Perceptions under the Bilingual 2030 Policy
text_snippet: Incorporating a Global Englishes Language Teaching ( GELT ) Perspective in Taiwanese Elementary Classrooms: Teachers' Perceptions under the Bilingual 2030 Policy Abstract This study examines the feasibility and pedagogical value of incorporating Global Englishes Language Teaching (GELT) into Taiwanese bilingual elementary English education, an area that remains critically underexplored despite the rapid global expansion of bilingual schooling. Focusing on a Taiwanese elementary school operating under the Bilingual 2030 policy, the study draws on semi‐structured interviews and focus group discussions to examine teachers' perceptions of bilingual teaching experiences and possibilities for integrating GELT principles into curricula. Findings reveal that bilingual education aligns well with GELT principles and serves as a catalyst for re‐shaping teachers' language ideologies. Despite institutional constraints, attachments to “native” English norms and societal expectations, participants expressed a strong willingness to adopt GELT. The study advances understanding of how GELT can be meaningfully implemented at the foundational stages of education and how bilingual education acts as a setting where language ideologies begin to take shape. title: Mixed‐Methods Research on English‐Medium Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
text_snippet: Mixed‐Methods Research on English‐Medium Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review Abstract With the rapid growth of research in English‐medium instruction (EMI) in higher education, much research has been conducted through qualitative and quantitative approaches. Yet, little attention was paid to the use of mixed‐methods research (MMR) in this field. Therefore, this systematic review aims to examine previous literature that adopted MMR in EMI research, specifically evaluating the methodology across three aspects: epistemological orientation and purpose, MMR question formulation, and MMR design. Among 136 studies identified, substantial methodological gaps were found across all three aspects. First, only seven studies explicitly stated an epistemological orientation whereas 27 studies provided explicit purpose terminology. Second, only six studies explicitly presented an integrative MMR question, while 112 studies provided qualitative and/or quantitative research questions, and 18 studies lacked explicit research questions. title: Pedagogical Translanguaging in Motion: Multimodal Mediation in Preservice Teachers' Storytelling with Young English Learners
text_snippet: Pedagogical Translanguaging in Motion: Multimodal Mediation in Preservice Teachers' Storytelling with Young English Learners Abstract Amid growing interest in multilingual pedagogies, translanguaging has increasingly been positioned as a response to monolingual teaching norms. Yet empirical accounts of what pedagogical translanguaging looks like in everyday classrooms—particularly in teaching English to young learners—remain limited. At the same time, although storytelling occupies a central place in young learner pedagogy, little research has examined how teachers mobilize linguistic and semiotic resources during storytelling lessons. Addressing both gaps, this study draws on the pedagogical translanguaging framework and the Dynamic Model of Multilingualism to investigate the evolving practices of eight preservice English teachers (PSTs) in Turkish state primary schools. The data set comprises 32 video‐recorded storytelling lessons over 8 weeks and follow‐up in‐depth interviews. Findings show that PSTs initially drew on shared linguistic repertoires to manage classroom interaction and scaffold story comprehension. title: Unveiling the AI Divide: A Comparative Study of Novice and Veteran EFL Teachers' Experience of Using Generative AI in Teaching
text_snippet: Unveiling the AI Divide: A Comparative Study of Novice and Veteran EFL Teachers' Experience of Using Generative AI in Teaching Abstract The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has brought both opportunities and challenges to the field of education. Within this evolving landscape, the emergence of the AI divide has become a pressing concern, particularly in teacher education and EFL instruction. This study developed a three‐level three‐factor conceptual framework to explore the AI divide through the dimensions of AI access, AI capability, and AI outcomes, while also considering technological, personal, and institutional influences. Using this framework, the study employed a comparative research design to examine how novice and veteran EFL teachers integrated AI differently in their teaching practices. The findings revealed that the AI divide between novice and veteran EFL teachers mostly occurred at the second level (AI capability) and third level (AI outcomes), rather than the first level (AI access). These disparities were shaped by a combination of technological, personal, and institutional factors, including perceived ease of use of AI, educational background, social support, and access to AI‐related professional development. title: Receptive Meaning‐Recall Knowledge of Derivational Morphology Among EFL Learners: A Case for L1 ‐Population‐Specific Assessment
text_snippet: Receptive Meaning‐Recall Knowledge of Derivational Morphology Among EFL Learners: A Case for L1 ‐Population‐Specific Assessment Abstract Vocabulary knowledge plays a crucial role in L2 proficiency, significantly impacting learners' reading comprehension. Although extensive research has explored whether knowledge of base words extends to recognition of derivational forms, results are inconsistent, especially among learners from non‐Indo‐European linguistic backgrounds. This study investigates the relationship between base word knowledge and comprehension of derivational forms among Arabic‐speaking EFL learners, examining how this relationship varies with proficiency. Using a meaning‐recall vocabulary test consisting of 30 base words and 46 derivational forms, data from 108 learners across four Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) levels (Below A1 to B1+) were analyzed through logistic mixed effects modeling. Results indicated that learners consistently performed better with base forms than derivations, with proficiency significantly moderating this relationship. title: Collaborative Development of a Research Agenda to Claim Language Teaching as a Site of Knowledge Production
text_snippet: Collaborative Development of a Research Agenda to Claim Language Teaching as a Site of Knowledge Production Abstract The development of research agendas is a crucial component of the process of reclaiming teaching as a site of knowledge production in language education research. However, in the TESOL field, the research agenda (RA) has traditionally been defined in relation to a gap between research and practice. Researchers often justify their work by highlighting significant disciplinary knowledge gaps. Therefore, when developing an RA, we must ask ourselves: (1) Whose interests does the RA serve? (2) Who should be involved in setting the RA? And (3) how can the RA be created and promoted? Engaging proactively with these questions encourages collaboration with practitioners and strengthens the link between research and practice. This approach helps us establish inclusive research agendas that benefit knowledge producers, including teachers, students, policymakers, and researchers. An RA should emerge from a collaborative and consultative process involving both researchers and teachers as practice researchers. title: Tracing the Change in the Status of a Language Teacher in University Governance through English Medium Instruction
text_snippet: Tracing the Change in the Status of a Language Teacher in University Governance through English Medium Instruction Abstract This article examines how a top‐down English medium instruction (EMI) decision changed a language teacher's status and participation in faculty governance in a graduate engineering school at a national university in Japan. Using a longitudinal single‐case design, the study follows one language teacher across the period from policy announcement to early rollout of EMI implementation. Data comprise three milestone interviews, audio‐recorded research‐practice meetings, reflective journals and implementation documents. Two main findings emerged. First, EMI acted as a catalyst for cultural change by raising the status of the language teacher in a setting where language support had been dismissed as a distraction from “real” engineering. Second, EMI granted the language teacher access to collaborate with a senior content teacher, who served as a gatekeeper to institutional leadership. This collaboration resulted in the formal establishment of EMI support provision and repositioned language support as a recognized component of engineering education. title: Fostering Fine‐Tuned Prompt Literacy for Multimodal Writing: A Systemic Functional Linguistics‐Informed Framework
text_snippet: Fostering Fine‐Tuned Prompt Literacy for Multimodal Writing: A Systemic Functional Linguistics‐Informed Framework Abstract The rise of GenAI‐powered image generation tools presents new opportunities for English learners to engage in digital multimodal composing (DMC) in both creative and critical ways. At the same time, it calls for a reconceptualization of DMC pedagogy in language education. In this article, we build on the concept of fine‐tuned prompt literacy (Kang & Yi, 2023) in the context of GenAI‐assisted multimodal writing and introduce a pedagogical framework informed by Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) to support its development and implementation. We conceptualize fine‐tuned prompt literacy at the intersection of multimodal literacy and GenAI literacy, emphasizing the need for students to envision meaningful GenAI outcomes and engage with GenAI tools critically and strategically. Drawing on our research on ESL students' photo essay creation with GenAI image generators, we show that separating instruction on multimodal and GenAI literacies may hinder students' process of creating multimodal resources in an intentional and rhetorically effective way. title: Effects of Motivational Interventions on EFL Learners' Learning Effort and Achievement: An L2 Motivational Self System Perspective
text_snippet: Effects of Motivational Interventions on EFL Learners' Learning Effort and Achievement: An L2 Motivational Self System Perspective Abstract Grounded in the L2 motivational self system theory, this quasi‐experimental study investigated the impact of three motivational interventions on two outcome measures: L2 learning effort and L2 achievement. A total of 391 Chinese junior secondary students were assigned to four conditions: a control group receiving no motivational instruction, and three experimental groups exposed to either traditional motivational strategies (MSs), vision‐based MSs, or a combined approach integrating both types of strategy. The effects of the interventions were assessed through questionnaires and tests administered at three time points to monitor changes in both outcome variables. The respective and relative effects of the interventions were determined by two‐way mixed design ANOVAs and post‐hoc pairwise comparisons. Results indicated that all three motivational treatments produced significantly positive effects on both outcome variables immediately following the interventions. title: Language Teacher Educator Identity, Wellbeing and Agency Nested in a Community of Practice: A Collaborative Autoethnography
text_snippet: Language Teacher Educator Identity, Wellbeing and Agency Nested in a Community of Practice: A Collaborative Autoethnography In this collaborative autoethnography, we, as three university‐based language teacher educators in Türkiye, explore how our community of practice (CoP) acted as a catalyst in navigating our identity tensions, boosting our wellbeing and contributing to our agency. Grounded in Wenger's (2009) framework of CoP, we embarked on a critical journey of navigating the tensions between our aspired and assigned identities as teacher educators in a dialogic and reflective third space of a CoP. The collegial space of our CoP enabled us to enact our agency and nurtured our wellbeing, embracing us in a safety net of solidarity and empowering us professionally in neoliberal academia. Conceptualizing the identity–wellbeing–agency triangle as a mutual, recursive and interdependent process nested in a CoP, this study showcases how LTEs reclaim their legitimacy, nourish their wellbeing and enact their agency in a safe dialogic space. Such a reconceptualization may bring new insights to LTEs in different contexts.

title: “Disciplinary Writing Is Like Playing with Legos”: Exploring a Multilingual International Student's Navigating Science Writing
text_snippet: “Disciplinary Writing Is Like Playing with Legos”: Exploring a Multilingual International Student's Navigating Science Writing Abstract This study explores the experiences of an undergraduate multilingual international student in becoming a science writer at a large public university. Taking the lenses of identity and investment, language socialization and multiliteracies, we address the question: How does a college‐aged multilingual science student navigate disciplinary writing over time? Interviews using talk around text based on the student's disciplinary writing samples over 3 years tracked his unique learning progress. Findings reveal he employed strategies including translingual, multimodal, and interdisciplinary practices and used GenAI to participate in disciplinary writing tasks, particularly when instruction and feedback were limited or harmful. The student gradually shifted from seeing disciplinary writing as a high‐stakes evaluation to understanding it as an agentive process of enacting future professional identity. By centering the lived experience of a multilingual writer, the study offers insights into the challenges and possibilities of disciplinary writing development in higher education (HE) classrooms. title: The Grit–Goal Relationship in Language Learning as a Dynamic Process: A Goal Self‐Concordance Perspective
text_snippet: The Grit–Goal Relationship in Language Learning as a Dynamic Process: A Goal Self‐Concordance Perspective Abstract Second language (L2) grit, a noncognitive ability that underlies the pursuit of language goals, has attracted growing scholarly attention. However, the grit–goal relationship—including why certain goals are set and how grittiness relates to their pursuit—remains underexplored, as L2 grit has largely been examined in relation to researcher‐selected proxies of goals. In this context, this mixed method study applied the goal self‐concordance framework (Henry, 2021) to analyze how goals aligned with one's sense of self and future direction are pursued, adjusted, and sometimes abandoned and how L2 grit relates to these processes. Questionnaire and interview data were collected from fourth‐year English majors in Japan ( N = 8) to examine how L2 grit related to their goal development histories. The findings suggest that (a) L2 grit levels do not always correspond to the attainment of self‐concordant goals and (b) attention to multiple layers of goals may be important for understanding which aspects of L2 grit are associated with the pursuit of self‐concordant goals.

title: Handwritten Versus Typed Notes: The Impact of Note‐Taking Modes in Second Language Listening Tests
text_snippet: Handwritten Versus Typed Notes: The Impact of Note‐Taking Modes in Second Language Listening Tests Abstract Technological advancements have influenced note‐taking practices in classrooms as well as their treatment in standardized language assessments. Many high‐stakes English listening tests (e.g., TOEFL iBT, IELTS) include varying note‐taking guidelines, often established without empirical support. This study examined the effects of note‐taking modes on listening performance and note content. A total of 305 L1‐Korean L2‐English adults were randomly assigned to handwriting ( n = 102), typing ( n = 102), or no note‐taking ( n = 101) conditions and completed TOEFL iBT lecture comprehension tasks. Linear regression results revealed no significant differences in overall test scores across modes. Uniform Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analyses indicated that one item favored handwriting and another favored typing, while non‐uniform DIF emerged for the same items only among lower‐ability participants. text_snippet: Integration in Qualitatively Oriented Mixed Methods Data Analysis: A Worked Example of a TESOL Graduate's Professional Experiences Abstract This paper focuses on integration in the data analysis of a qualitatively oriented mixed methods study, illustrating this process through a worked example of interactions with social actors shaping a TESOL graduate's professional experiences. We developed and integrated layered descriptions and interpretations using the following strategies: (1) quantitative indicators and qualitative structural analysis to detail network features of visual data and facilitate further analysis and (2) reflexive thematic analysis procedures and qualitative comparative analysis strategies to explore patterns within the textual data. These analyses were brought together to develop a holistic understanding of network features and associated practices, as well as their influence on the TESOL graduate's professional experiences. text_snippet: Exploring Digital Multimodal Ensembles and Monomodal Expository Essays: From Author Performance to Reader Perspectives Abstract Although many teacher/researchers have expressed enthusiasm about the benefits of digital multimodal literacies, empirical evidence of the value of engagement with multimodal ensembles for L2 students as authors and readers is limited. This study compared the quality of digital multimodal composing (DMC) and monomodal writing and explored the impact of both on readers' new knowledge building. title: GenAI ‐Assisted Digital Multimodal Composing in TESOL Teacher Education
text_snippet: GenAI ‐Assisted Digital Multimodal Composing in TESOL Teacher Education Abstract This study explored how pre‐service TESOL teachers integrated GenAI tools into a Digital Multimodal Composing (DMC) project, composing a website, at a Hong Kong university. Specifically, it explored their decision‐making and cognitive engagement in the DMC process when they had autonomy in the use of GenAI tools. Drawing on a social practice perspective of literacy, the research explores how GenAI supports or complicates multimodal composing and the professional learning outcomes for TESOL pre‐service teachers. Data were collected through group and individual interviews with stimulated recall and analysis of group project websites. This inquiry illustrates how such a lens offers possibilities for integrating African systems of knowing and being with digital multimodal resources toward envisioning asset‐based education for African and African immigrant children. title: Rethinking Quality in L2 Research Synthesis: Collective Initiative Toward Developing Validated Tools to Assess Methodological Rigor of Primary Studies
text_snippet: Rethinking Quality in L2 Research Synthesis: Collective Initiative Toward Developing Validated Tools to Assess Methodological Rigor of Primary Studies Abstract This Research Issues paper calls for the development and validation of field‐specific appraisal tools for the methodological rigor of primary studies included in research syntheses. Adopting an instrumental case study design, this investigation used thematic analysis and multimodal content analysis (MMCA) to examine 68 video presentations. text_snippet: “Show Me How You Can Practice That”: Multimodal Socioemotional Instruction in a Dual Language Bilingual Education Preschool Abstract When providing socioemotional instruction to emergent bilingual children, preschool teachers are responsible for helping them navigate cultural and linguistic intersections of socioemotional learning. Teachers' multimodal practices may support that instruction, given that the children's socioemotional learning is an emotional, physical, and psychological endeavor. We employ CASEL's framework to identify socioemotional competencies as comprising self‐awareness, self‐management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision‐making. title: Early‐Career EFL Researchers' Academic Identity Evolving through Online Translanguaging Training
text_snippet: Early‐Career EFL Researchers' Academic Identity Evolving through Online Translanguaging Training Abstract This study explores the evolution of early‐career EFL researchers' academic identity through online translanguaging training. Drawing on van Veen and Sleegers' (2009) conceptual framework and integrating complexity theory, translanguaging theory, and the ecological perspective, this qualitative research examines the experiences of 20 Turkish early‐career EFL researchers from diverse institutional and geographic contexts. Data were collected through pre‐ and post‐training interviews and reflective journals, analyzed via abductive methods. Findings reveal that translanguaging training impacts academic identity across micro, meso, and exo/macro layers, with participants exhibiting varying degrees of transformation. Three main groups emerged: translanguaging pioneers and explorers, and a small grouping of traditionalists; furthermore, two participants were classed as borderline explorer/pioneers, suggesting that categories were overlapping and fluid rather than fixed. title: Investigating Filipino College Teachers' Views on Aestheticizing the English Accent in ELT
text_snippet: Investigating Filipino College Teachers' Views on Aestheticizing the English Accent in ELT Abstract Although English language teaching (ELT) increasingly recognizes the legitimacy of diverse Englishes, accent remains a powerful basis for judging teachers' competence, credibility, and professional value. This study examines how Filipino college teachers view the aestheticization of English accents in ELT and how they negotiate their own accents in relation to other English varieties. Using a qualitative design, the study drew on semi‐structured online interviews with 16 Filipino college English teachers from different higher education institutions in the Philippines. The data were analyzed thematically through the lenses of language aesthetics as language ideology, metapragmatic distance, and Unequal Englishes. Findings show that teachers often define a ‘good‐sounding’ accent in terms of intelligibility, clarity, student understanding, and classroom usefulness rather than ‘native’‐like imitation. At the same time, they recognize the continuing prestige of Americanized, ‘neutral,’ and ‘standard’ accents as forms of symbolic and market value. title: Madrasa Ideologies of English in Bangladesh: Questioning ELT ‐Aid and Post‐9/11 De‐Islamization
text_snippet: Madrasa Ideologies of English in Bangladesh: Questioning ELT ‐Aid and Post‐9/11 De‐Islamization Abstract External donors increasingly promote English as a notionally value‐neutral language of socioeconomic advancements in the Muslim South, overlooking local ideological diversities. Furthermore, national and Western forces deploy English as a tool to de‐Islamize madrasas (Islamic educational institutes) in the post‐9/11 world for global peace. Given that the madrasa ideologies of English are scarcely represented in TESOL, this paper presents such ideologies from a Bangladeshi madrasa to critically examine ELT‐aid projects and the efforts to moderate madrasas through English. Data were collected from a traditional Qawmi madrasa in rural Bangladesh employing a linguistic ethnography under a doctoral project. The findings show that people in the madrasa navigate English within various spiritual, historical, and cultural ideological dynamics but identify the language as crucial for furthering Islam. title: Leveraging GenAI for Automated Feedback on Source‐Based Writing: A Three‐Stage Model
text_snippet: Leveraging GenAI for Automated Feedback on Source‐Based Writing: A Three‐Stage Model Abstract Writing from multiple sources is a critical skill that requires both reading and writing abilities. It involves comprehending and evaluating source texts while synthesizing information across them. Due to these demands, feedback on such writing typically relies on teachers, who must consider the source texts during evaluation. Although technological tools have been introduced to support teacher feedback, existing automated systems often inadequately assess source‐based writing, as they focus solely on students' final texts and neglect the source texts, leading to invalid assessments. The advent of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), capable of understanding and analyzing large volumes of text simultaneously, offers a promising solution. In this article, we propose a three‐stage GenAI‐enabled feedback model for source‐based writing. This model aligns with the key stages of the source‐based reading‐to‐writing process: evaluating individual sources, mapping multiple sources, and synthesizing information across sources. title: Learner Engagement in L2 Vocabulary Learning through Communicative Tasks: Comparing Learner‐ and Teacher‐Generated Content
text_snippet: Learner Engagement in L2 Vocabulary Learning through Communicative Tasks: Comparing Learner‐ and Teacher‐Generated Content Abstract This study examined how task design, task motivation, and learner engagement influenced L2 vocabulary learning by comparing learner‐generated content (LGC) and teacher‐generated content (TGC) in a classroom setting. One hundred sixty‐three Japanese high school students from five intact classes were assigned to LGC, TGC, or a test‐only control group, and the two treatment groups completed two decision‐making tasks. Vocabulary learning was assessed using form recall, meaning recall, and a lexicosemantic judgment task (LJT) with a pretest–posttest design. Task motivation (expectancies, value, and cost) was measured prior to Task 1, and learner engagement (cognitive, social, and emotional) was measured after Task 2. Generalized linear mixed‐effects models showed that the LGC group outperformed the TGC group on form recall (large effect) and meaning recall (medium effect), whereas no group difference emerged for LJT performance. title: Supporting Pathways into College and Careers: The Case of Adult Education ESL in Community Colleges
text_snippet: Supporting Pathways into College and Careers: The Case of Adult Education ESL in Community Colleges Abstract Research has increasingly focused on the importance of college preparation and career and technical education (CTE) for multilingual learners (MLs), many of them classified as “English Learners,” in K‐12 schools. Less attention, however, has been paid to the collegiate and professional aspirations of another significant population of MLs in the United States: those studying ESL in adult education programs. This paper examines how structural and systemic barriers impede access to opportunities for college and career readiness (CCR) for students enrolled in adult ESL programs in community colleges, how personnel at one large urban community college district understood and attempted to counter those barriers, and how institutional habitus and doxa (taken‐for‐granted assumptions and practices) shaped those attempts. title: Assessment of Digital Multimodal Composing: Toward Ethical and Responsible Use of Generative AI
text_snippet: Assessment of Digital Multimodal Composing: Toward Ethical and Responsible Use of Generative AI Abstract This Research Issues paper outlines the theoretical and practical foundations for assessing GenAI‐mediated DMC, with a particular focus on frameworks for ethical authorship, diverse assessment approaches and methods, and flexible quality criteria and rubrics. Drawing on theoretical traditions including social semiotics, systemic functional linguistics, multiliteracies, and sociocultural theories, we have emphasized the importance of ethical and responsible authorship in AI‐mediated composition. In particular, we argue that fine‐tuned prompt literacy and transpositional grammar allow learners to interact critically and creatively with GenAI tools, enabling them to navigate complex semiotic environments while maintaining agency and ethical authorship. Successful assessment in this context demands flexible, context‐sensitive models that reflect the evolving nature of GenAI‐mediated DMC. title: “Your English Sounds Almost British”: Everyday Linguicism and Racialized Subjectivity of an International Student in Hong Kong
text_snippet: “Your English Sounds Almost British”: Everyday Linguicism and Racialized Subjectivity of an International Student in Hong Kong Abstract This article examines how everyday linguicism and racism shape the academic and social experiences of international students in Hong Kong, focusing on the racialized subjectivity of a South Asian graduate student. Although research on international students has mainly focused on Western higher education, little attention has been paid to the lived realities faced by racialized students in multilingual, postcolonial Asian contexts. Through a single in‐depth case study, the analysis shows how mobility repositions students within racialized and linguicized hierarchies: English‐medium classrooms offer academic access yet coexist with campus infrastructures dominated by Cantonese and Mandarin that structurally exclude nonlocal speakers; raciolinguistic ideologies portray South Asian English speakers as perpetually deficient, even when they are proficient; and gendered expectations place representational and reproductive scrutiny on women students. text_snippet: Incidental Acquisition of Multiword Expressions Through Repeated Viewing: Sequential Use of L1 and L2 Captions Abstract Repeated viewing is reportedly a common learning and pedagogical strategy among autonomous second language (L2) learners and language teachers. This experimental study examined the extent to which sequential captioning use facilitates the acquisition of multiword expressions (MWEs) through repeated viewing under incidental learning conditions. A total of 109 Chinese‐speaking learners of English were randomly allocated to three experimental groups and one control group. title: Innovating EFL Writing Through Collaborative Digital Multimodal Composing
text_snippet: Innovating EFL Writing Through Collaborative Digital Multimodal Composing Abstract Given the evolving landscape of digital and multimodal communication, collaborative digital multimodal composing (DMC) has emerged as a promising pedagogical approach for enhancing second language learning. Despite its advocacy in educational contexts, the implementation of collaborative DMC in EFL classrooms remains largely underexplored. The current study aims to address this gap by exploring an EFL teacher's attempts at collaborative DMC in an English writing course for first‐year undergraduates, focusing on the practical application of this innovative approach and the perceived benefits experienced by both students and the instructor. Data were collected through reflective journals from 30 course participants, semi‐structured interviews with six focal students and the course instructor, DMC products, and classroom documents. title: Implementing Argument‐Based Validity in Second Language Research on Individual Differences
text_snippet: Implementing Argument‐Based Validity in Second Language Research on Individual Differences Abstract Quantitative meta‐syntheses focusing on the psychometric properties of measurement tools in second and foreign language (L2) individual differences (ID) research have drawn scholars' attention to the quality of data collection instruments (Plonsky & Derrick, 2016; Sudina, 2023). In many primary L2 ID studies systematically reviewed to date, little attention has been given to instrument validity, which may lead to unsubstantiated inferences and unjustifiable conclusions. Although some attempts have been made to raise awareness of the importance of validity evidence for certain constructs (e.g., language learning motivation; see Al‐Hoorie, Hiver, & In'nami, 2024; Papi & Teimouri, 2025), an overarching theoretical and methodological validation framework that L2 ID researchers could rely on appears to be missing. In our theoretical paper, we aim to provide scaffolding for measurement in L2 ID studies by drawing on argument‐based validation (ABV) practices in other areas of applied linguistics (Chapelle, 2021; Kane, 2013; for a recent synthesis, see Zhang & Aryadoust, 2022). For illustrative purposes, we used a quantitative measure with documented psychometric characteristics.

text_snippet: Designing Feedback and Assessment for GenAI ‐Assisted Digital Multimodal Composition in L2 Abstract The rapidly evolving use of GenAI leads to a crucial need for new approaches to instruction and assessment of language skills in DMC tasks. The study adopted a convergent mixed‐methods design within an 11‐week action research framework. The study was conducted with 12 Turkish tertiary‐level L2 learners based on a process‐genre pedagogy to design and test a novel assessment framework. title: Trauma in TESOL : Theoretical, Methodological, and Pedagogical Perspectives
text_snippet: Trauma in TESOL : Theoretical, Methodological, and Pedagogical Perspectives Abstract This editorial introduction frames the special issue ‘Trauma in TESOL: Theoretical, Methodological, and Pedagogical Perspectives’ by advancing a decolonial, feminist, and socially grounded orientation to trauma in language education. Moving beyond dominant medicalized models that treat trauma as an individual, pathological condition, we conceptualize trauma as a relational, sociopolitical, and affective phenomenon that is mediated through language and embedded in broader structures of power, inequality, and historical violence. We argue that the nexus between trauma and language is inextricable: while trauma is often described as “unspeakable,” processes of narrating, representing, and engaging with traumatic experience through language are central to healing, resistance, and identity reconstruction. The contributions in this issue, across both research articles and a Forum section, extend TESOL scholarship by broadening the range of traumatic contexts examined, foregrounding the experiences of both learners and teachers, and demonstrating how pedagogical practices, care work, and communicative activity are deeply interconnected. title: Using Virtual Exchange for Teaching BELF Pragmatics: Developing an Online Negotiation Activity
text_snippet: Using Virtual Exchange for Teaching BELF Pragmatics: Developing an Online Negotiation Activity Abstract Teaching Business English (BE) is experiencing a paradigm shift to reflect the communicative needs of the global workplace. With the majority of interactions in English now taking place among multilingual speakers, there are increasing calls to integrate perspectives of English as a business lingua franca (BELF) into English language and business communication teaching. Particularly, the teaching of BELF pragmatics is lacking in theoretical discussion and in tested, practical solutions to be applied in the classroom. To address this gap, we have capitalized on virtual exchanges (VE) and built an online negotiation activity targeted at practicing BELF‐pragmatic strategies. This paper reports on the process of developing the activity through an action research project over three semesters into a viable and pedagogically meaningful teaching component. title: Between Exploration and Caution: Psychological Need Profiles in AI Integration Among Chinese University EFL Teachers
text_snippet: Between Exploration and Caution: Psychological Need Profiles in AI Integration Among Chinese University EFL Teachers Abstract As AI becomes increasingly integrated into language education, teachers' responses to AI‐integrated teaching deserve closer attention. Guided by Self‐Determination Theory, this study employed an explanatory sequential mixed methods design to examine how Chinese university EFL teachers' basic psychological need profiles were associated with their AI use, perceived school support, and perceived professional roles. In the quantitative phase, survey data from 408 teachers were analyzed through latent profile analysis, identifying three profiles: “Motivation‐Constrained”, “Autonomy‐Driven”, and “Relationally Anchored”. In the qualitative phase, interviews with nine teachers selected from these profiles were used to explain profile‐specific patterns. Autonomy‐Driven teachers reported the highest levels of AI use and perceived school support and positioned themselves as instructional designers. title: Introducing and Evaluating a Measure of Lexical Diversity Across Word Classes
text_snippet: Introducing and Evaluating a Measure of Lexical Diversity Across Word Classes Abstract Lexical diversity (LD) has been shown to be a strong predictor of second language (L2) proficiency. However, most current indices combine all word classes into a single measure and thus only capture the broadest patterns of lexical variation. In addition, researchers interested in examining usage patterns across word classes currently lack access to measures of LD that are both more linguistically interpretable and robust to text length. In response to these issues, this paper introduces a methodology for examining part‐of‐speech (POS)‐specific LD indices (e.g., verb and noun diversity) that apply the moving‐average type‐token ratio (MATTR), a measure validated for its stability across text lengths and reliability in shorter texts. We also evaluate these measures by comparing them to traditional, so‐called omnibus LD measures for interpreting L2 corpus data. title: Longitudinal Tracking of Persistence in Other‐Repair Practices in an Audio‐Mediated English Private Tutoring Setting
text_snippet: Longitudinal Tracking of Persistence in Other‐Repair Practices in an Audio‐Mediated English Private Tutoring Setting Abstract Private tutoring—or shadow education—has received ample scholarly attention due to increasing demand from parents for reasons of social mobility in ESL/EFL contexts. Referred to as English private tutoring (EPT) for language learning purposes, this type of non‐formal education shares certain features of formal education like content and classroom interactional practices such as teachers' management of turn‐taking and repair practices. However, despite the surge of EPT across the globe, how tutors manage other‐repair, a regular classroom interactional and pedagogical practice, in EPT settings remains unexamined. title: Communicative Drills: The Impact of Communicative Intent on Oral Proficiency
text_snippet: Communicative Drills: The Impact of Communicative Intent on Oral Proficiency Abstract This exploratory study investigated the role of communicative intent in second language (L2) oral practice by comparing communicative and meaningful drills. English language learners played a game designed to elicit repeated use of the second conditional. One group played the real game as a communicative drill across two sessions, while the other group first played a simulated, non‐communicative version of the game as a meaningful drill before engaging in the real game. Both drills involved identical output opportunities and feedback, differing only in whether learners chose their own messages and required their interlocutor's understanding. Utterances were rated using a rubric and mean ratings were compared across days and groups. Results showed no difference in language quality on the first day, but the communicative‐first group demonstrated significantly higher ratings and improvement on the second day. These findings provide empirical support for the important role of communicative intent in L2 practice. Implications for pedagogy and research methodology are discussed.

title: From Pedagogy to Practice: Using Microlearning to Prepare Teachers for GenAI and Digital Multimodal Composition
text_snippet: From Pedagogy to Practice: Using Microlearning to Prepare Teachers for GenAI and Digital Multimodal Composition Abstract This teaching article explores how microlearning can support TESOL educators in developing the pedagogical and emotional capacities needed to use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools to design and evaluate digital multimodal compositions (DMC). Grounded in sociocultural theory and teacher development literature, it proposes microlearning as a flexible, scalable and emotionally responsive professional development (PD) model. Short, focused microlearning modules can deliver just‐in‐time learning, reduce cognitive overload and build confidence through guided practice. Moving from pedagogical principles to classroom practice, drawing on microlearning design principles and offering sample modules, the article shows how GenAI‐enhanced microlearning PD can help TESOL educators to develop progressive competence in digital multimodal composition while maintaining the agency to integrate, constrain or decline GenAI use. The article also addresses the emotional labor associated with technological change, showing that GenAI‐enhanced microlearning PD offers a sustainable path for TESOL educators to adapt to GenAI‐driven shifts in literacy, authorship and classroom practice.
